\section{Abstract}\label{abstract}

\textbf{Background.} A fixed price is asymptotically optimal for selling
a fixed perishable stock as expected sales grow, leaving open what
simple dynamic rules gain or lose at moderate scale. \textbf{Question.}
In a simulated market with 100 units, 60 periods, two buyer segments and
demand shocks, does an occupancy rule (OCC) or a demand-responsive rule
(DRP) change expected revenue relative to the best fixed price (FIX)
under equal tuning budgets and identical demand streams?
\textbf{Method.} Three experiments were frozen before any evaluation
stream existed: a base comparison (EXP-001), a 3 x 3 grid of valuation
dispersion and demand-to-capacity ratio (EXP-002) and a misspecification
test (EXP-003), with 4,000 paired evaluation streams per cell (925,000
simulated seasons, none failed). \textbf{Results.} At the base cell, OCC
and DRP earn +407.0 (97.5\% interval {[}373.2, 440.2{]}, +3.47\%) and
+462.1 ({[}426.0, 498.1{]}, +3.94\%) currency units per season more than
FIX. The sign is not general: all 18 EXP-002 contrasts reject the null
(Holm), but 8 are negative, including every loose-capacity cell (DRP
down to -11.41\%). The preregistered invalidation rule is not triggered
by moderate demand shifts, but the rules lose at 0.6 times the forecast
demand, and against a fixed price re-tuned to the true demand their
relevant gains are confined to demand above the forecast (and, for OCC,
reversed arrivals). \textbf{Conclusion.} Within this model, the two
simple rules beat a well-tuned fixed price when stock is scarce relative
to demand or demand exceeds the forecast, and lose when capacity is
loose; no general advantage is supported.

\section{Keywords}\label{keywords}

dynamic pricing; revenue management; perishable inventory; simulation;
preregistration; reproducibility

\section{1. Introduction}\label{introduction}

Sellers of perishable capacity, such as seats or rooms, face a finite
selling horizon after which unsold units are worth nothing. A price that
is too low sells out before the high-valuation buyers arrive; a price
that is too high leaves units unsold at the deadline. Dynamic pricing
changes the price over the horizon in response to the remaining stock,
the remaining time or the observed sales. Gallego and van Ryzin (1994)
showed for a single product under price-sensitive stochastic demand that
the optimal price depends on remaining stock and remaining time, and
that simple fixed-price policies are asymptotically optimal as the
volume of expected sales tends to infinity. A well-tuned fixed price is
therefore a principled baseline, and the open question at moderate scale
is empirical: how much do simple, model-free dynamic rules gain or lose
against it, and under which market conditions?

This manuscript answers that question for one transparent synthetic
market. The research question is the one set for the project: ``How do
demand and inventory policies affect prices and availability in a
simulated market?'' It is made operational as follows.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{RQ1 (EXP-001).} At the base scenario, does a tuned occupancy
  rule or a tuned demand-responsive rule change expected revenue per
  selling season relative to the tuned fixed price, under identical
  demand streams and equal tuning budgets?
\item
  \textbf{RQ2.} How do the policies differ in sell-through,
  availability, price volatility and a consumer surplus proxy?
\item
  \textbf{RQ3 (EXP-002).} How do the differences depend on valuation
  dispersion (which sets price elasticity) and on demand-to-capacity
  tightness?
\item
  \textbf{RQ4 (EXP-003).} Does the base comparison survive
  misspecification of the demand used for tuning?
\end{itemize}

The primary hypotheses are nondirectional: for
\(j \in \{\text{OCC}, \text{DRP}\}\), \(H_0: \Delta_j = 0\) against
\(H_1: \Delta_j \neq 0\), where \(\Delta_j\) is the expected paired
revenue difference against the tuned fixed price. The planning
expectation, stated before the freeze and not a hypothesis, was a small
gain of at most 5\% of fixed-price revenue at this scale.

The contributions are the following.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  A preregistered comparison of a fixed price and two simple dynamic
  rule families under an equal 36-configuration tuning budget, exactly
  matched demand streams and held-out evaluation streams, with every
  protocol and configuration frozen by hash before execution.
\item
  A complete report of a mixed-sign result: the dynamic rules gain at
  the base cell and in tight markets and lose in every loose-capacity
  cell.
\item
  A pre-specified misspecification analysis, reported together with its
  limits as an invalidation test.
\item
  An evidence audit and a challenge pass that revise two interpretations
  of the experiment reports, with every change recorded.
\end{enumerate}

No novelty claim is made. The literature search was targeted, not
systematic (Section 2).

\section{2. Related work}\label{related-work}

The search behind this section was targeted, and each source is marked
by what was actually read (\texttt{research/literature\_review.md}).
Three sources were checked against their full text (the cited section is
given in \texttt{research/literature\_review.md}); Elmaghraby and
Keskinocak (2003) was read as an abstract only and is cited only for
what the abstract states.

\textbf{Finite-horizon pricing of a fixed stock.} Gallego and van Ryzin
(1994; full text, Theorems 1 and 3) formulate the sale of a fixed stock
over a finite horizon under price-sensitive stochastic demand as an
intensity-control problem. They show that the optimal price is monotone
in remaining stock and remaining time, derive a deterministic upper
bound on expected revenue and prove that simple fixed-price policies are
asymptotically optimal as the volume of expected sales tends to
infinity. Their multiproduct extension (Gallego and van Ryzin, 1997;
full text, Section 5) applies a similar deterministic bound to network
yield management. FARE does not test the asymptotic regime: it fixes the
stock at 100 units and asks what simple rules do at that scale.

\textbf{Reviews and practice.} Elmaghraby and Keskinocak (2003; abstract
only) review dynamic pricing in the presence of inventory considerations
and identify industries with short-run fixed, perishable capacity, such
as airlines and hotels, as the classical setting. FARE borrows only this
framing. It makes no claim about any airline, hotel or proprietary
pricing system.

\textbf{Strategic buyers.} Su (2007; full text of the author's version,
Sections 5 and 6) shows that when customers differ in valuation and
patience and time their purchases, the optimal price path and its
effects on revenue and welfare change. FARE assumes myopic buyers, so
its results do not extend to strategic buyers.

\textbf{Learning and uncertainty.} Work on dynamic pricing under demand
uncertainty and learning exists (for example den Boer's 2013 doctoral
thesis), but only the front matter of that thesis was opened, so it is
not cited for content here.

\textbf{Position of this study.} FARE is a replication-style extension,
not new theory. It takes the fixed price that theory recommends as the
baseline, adds two rule families that a practitioner could tune without
a demand model, and asks a narrow empirical question under a frozen
protocol. Whether a comparable open, preregistered study exists was not
established.

\section{3. Background and formal
model}\label{background-and-formal-model}

The full specification is in \texttt{research/protocol.md} (frozen v1.0,
SHA-256 \texttt{d4b7c1e0...}). Table 1 lists the base parameters.

\textbf{Market.} Periods \(t = 1, \dots, T\) with \(T = 60\). Stock
\(x_t\) starts at \(x_1 = C = 100\) units; units unsold after period
\(T\) perish with zero salvage. Two buyer segments, \(s \in \{L, H\}\),
have shares \(w_L = 0.7\) and \(w_H = 0.3\). Expected arrivals over the
horizon are \(A = \kappa C\) with base \(\kappa = 2.0\). Segment arrival
profiles are linear and normalised: \(a_L(t) \propto T + 1 - t\) (early)
and \(a_H(t) \propto t\) (late). A stream-level multiplier
\(M \sim \text{LogNormal}(-\sigma_M^2/2, \sigma_M)\) with
\(\sigma_M = 0.25\) and three-period surges (start probability 0.05 per
period, intensity factor 1.8, non-compounding) create demand shocks.
Arrivals are
\(N_{s,t} \sim \text{Poisson}(M A w_s a_s(t) \cdot \text{surge}_t)\) and
valuations are \(v \sim \text{LogNormal}(\ln m_s, \sigma_v)\) with
\(m_L = 100\), \(m_H = 200\) (abstract currency units) and base
\(\sigma_v = 0.5\). Buyers are myopic with unit demand: a buyer arriving
in period \(t\) buys if \(v \geq p_t\) and \(x > 0\) and otherwise
leaves. Prices are bounded in \([30, 600]\).

Because buyers are myopic, the demand stream does not depend on the
policy. Each stream is generated once and replayed under every policy
(common random numbers), so policy comparisons are exactly paired.

\textbf{Policies.} With \(f_t = (C - x_t)/C\) the fraction sold and
\(e_t = (t-1)/T\) the fraction of the horizon elapsed:

\[\text{FIX}(p):\; p_t = p, \qquad \text{OCC}(p_0, k):\; p_t = \operatorname{clip}\big(p_0\, e^{k (f_t - e_t)},\, 30,\, 600\big).\]

DRP\((p_0, \eta)\) starts at \(p_1 = p_0\), keeps an exponentially
weighted average \(\hat r\) of units sold per period (weight 0.3,
initialised at \(C/T\)), computes the target rate
\(r^*_t = x_t / (T - t + 1)\) and updates

\[p_{t+1} = \operatorname{clip}\Big(p_t \Big(\frac{\hat r + 0.5}{r^*_t + 0.5}\Big)^{\eta},\, 30,\, 600\Big).\]

Both rules nest the fixed price: \(k = 0\) gives FIX\((p_0)\) and
\(\eta = 0\) gives FIX\((p_0)\).

\textbf{Tuning.} Each family has 36 configurations, all evaluated on the
same 500 tuning streams, and the configuration with the highest mean
revenue is selected. FIX uses 36 geometric prices from 40 to 400. OCC
and DRP use 6 geometric starting prices \(p_0\) from 40 to 400 times 6
sensitivity values: \(k \in \{0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8\}\) and
\(\eta \in \{0.025, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0\}\). The 6 starting prices
are also FIX prices. Tuning and evaluation streams are disjoint.

\textbf{Estimand.} For \(j \in \{\text{OCC}, \text{DRP}\}\),

\[\Delta_j = \mathbb{E}\big[R(j^*, S) - R(\text{FIX}^*, S)\big],\]

the expected paired revenue difference per evaluation stream \(S\),
where \(j^*\) and FIX\(^*\) are the tuned policies. The relative effect
is \(\Delta_j / \mathbb{E}[R(\text{FIX}^*, S)]\).

\textbf{Complexity.} The simulator sorts the valuations within each
period and locates the sale cut-off by bisection; a naive buyer-by-buyer
simulator serves as a differential-test oracle. The full confirmatory
matrix of 925,000 runs took 34.5 s, 268.8 s and 161.1 s for the three
experiments on a shared laptop (runtime is not a result).

\section{4. Methods}\label{methods}

\subsection{4.1 Design and protocol
registration}\label{design-and-protocol-registration}

The study protocol and the three experiment protocols were written
before any confirmatory run and frozen by the owner on 2026-11-24 as
v1.0 after two rounds of amendments, with SHA-256 hashes of every
protocol and confirmatory configuration recorded in
\texttt{research/freeze.json}. The runner refuses any configuration or
protocol whose hash differs from the freeze record. Before the freeze,
exploratory values of the primary contrast had been computed on tuning
streams only (n = 50 per cell, an earlier grid); they are disclosed in
the freeze record (C4). The owner chose the final tuning grids with
these values available, which is a disclosed forking-paths risk on the
grid choice. No evaluation stream was generated before the freeze.

All three experiments are confirmatory. The checks in Section 5.4 were
computed during interpretation (M4), after the results were seen; they
are exploratory and never change a frozen verdict.

\subsection{4.2 Simulated market and
data}\label{simulated-market-and-data}

All data are synthetic (no dataset was downloaded). Streams are
generated by
\texttt{numpy.random.SeedSequence(entropy\ =\ 20261124,\ spawn\_key\ =\ (experiment,\ cell,\ role,\ index))},
with role 0 for tuning (indices 0 to 499) and role 1 for evaluation
(indices 0 to 3999). Each run records its seed key and the SHA-256 of
its stream.

\subsection{4.3 Experiments, controls and
baselines}\label{experiments-controls-and-baselines}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{EXP-001} (base cell). FIX, OCC and DRP tuned and evaluated on
  4,000 streams. A tuning-grid sensitivity arm FIX6 re-tunes FIX on the
  6 starting prices available to the rules.
\item
  \textbf{EXP-002} (elasticity and tightness).
  \(\sigma_v \in \{0.25, 0.5, 1.0\}\) times
  \(\kappa \in \{1.0, 2.0, 4.0\}\), 9 cells, each re-tuned (a fixed
  price tuned elsewhere would be a strawman) and evaluated on 4,000
  streams.
\item
  \textbf{EXP-003} (misspecification). The policies tuned at the base
  cell are evaluated without re-tuning on 6 cells: demand level times
  0.6, 0.8, 1.25 and 1.6, reversed segment arrival order, and no shocks.
  A fixed price re-tuned on each cell's own tuning streams is a
  reference that separates the cost of misspecification from policy
  structure.
\end{itemize}

The controls are common random numbers, the equal tuning budget,
disjoint tuning and evaluation streams, and the tested nesting property
(\(k = 0\) and \(\eta = 0\) reproduce FIX exactly).

\subsection{4.4 Metrics}\label{metrics}

Revenue per season (primary, currency units). Secondary and descriptive:
sell-through (units sold / \(C\)), availability (share of arriving
buyers who found stock; 1 when no buyer arrived), stock-out period,
price volatility \(\frac{1}{T-1}\sum_{t=2}^{T}|\ln p_t - \ln p_{t-1}|\),
a consumer surplus proxy \(\sum_i (v_i - p_{\text{paid},i})\) and a
total surplus proxy (revenue plus consumer surplus proxy; no costs are
modelled). The point purchase elasticity at the tuned fixed price is
reported per EXP-002 cell.

\subsection{4.5 Statistical analysis}\label{statistical-analysis}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{EXP-001.} \(H_0^j\) is rejected when the Bonferroni-adjusted
  97.5\% stream-level paired percentile bootstrap interval (10,000
  resamples, seed 20261124) excludes 0. Effects are classified against a
  smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) of 1\% of mean FIX\(^*\)
  revenue: detectable and practically relevant, detectable but below the
  SESOI, practically equivalent (interval inside \(\pm\) SESOI) or
  inconclusive. Paired \(t\) intervals are a cross-check. If the
  contrast against FIX6 changes sign or class, the result is attributed
  to grid resolution.
\item
  \textbf{EXP-002.} A paired sign-flip permutation test per contrast
  (10,000 permutations), Holm adjustment over the 18 contrasts at
  family-wise \(\alpha = 0.05\), paired bootstrap 95\% intervals.
  Interaction contrasts \(\Delta(\kappa = 4) - \Delta(\kappa = 1)\) per
  \(\sigma_v\) use an independent stratified bootstrap (descriptive).
\item
  \textbf{EXP-003.} Paired bootstrap 95\% intervals per cell
  (descriptive), with a pre-specified invalidation rule: if, at demand
  times 0.8 or 1.25, the 95\% interval of \(\Delta_{j,c}\) lies entirely
  on the opposite side of zero from the EXP-001 estimate, the EXP-001
  result for \(j\) is reported as specific to correct specification.
\item
  \textbf{Sample size.} 4,000 evaluation streams per cell. A
  tuning-stream pilot put the requirement for the 1\% SESOI at two-sided
  \(\alpha = 0.025\) and power 0.89 between 384 and 3,435 streams across
  cells. The sample size was fixed at the freeze; there were no interim
  looks and no outcome-based exclusions.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{4.6 Reproducibility}\label{reproducibility}

Every confirmatory run set records the git revision (\texttt{4204eac},
no tracked file modified), the protocol and configuration hashes, the
data manifest hash, the environment (Python 3.12.1, numpy 2.5.4, Apple
M1 Pro, macOS 15.3.1), runtime and peak memory. Raw per-run outputs
(21.5 MB, 147.8 MB and 132.2 MB) are git-ignored and regenerable; their
SHA-256 hashes, the aggregate tables and the figures are committed under
\texttt{research/experiments/EXP-NNN/}. Section 10 gives the commands.

\section{5. Results}\label{results}

All 925,000 planned runs completed (EXP-001: 73,000; EXP-002: 594,000;
EXP-003: 258,000) and none failed or was dropped. Every number below
comes from the committed files named in each table caption. The evidence
audit (\texttt{research/publication/evidence\_audit.md}) recomputed
every committed arm summary and contrast from the raw outputs with zero
discrepancy.

FIX(139.61), OCC(\(p_0\) = 159.24, \(k\) = 4) and DRP(\(p_0\) = 100.48,
\(\eta\) = 0.1).

(2,667.8) for OCC and 12,177.6 (2,574.6) for DRP. Pairing matters: the
SDs of the paired differences are 951.7 and 1,013.7.

lower (128.78 and 123.23 against 139.61). Price volatility is 0.0439
(OCC) and 0.0288 (DRP) per period, and zero for FIX by construction.

\subsection{5.2 EXP-002: elasticity and tightness
(RQ3)}\label{exp-002-elasticity-and-tightness-rq3}

All 18 contrasts reject \(H_0\) after Holm adjustment (every raw
sign-flip \(p\) is at the permutation floor 1/10001, so every Holm value
of 0.0018 is a bound). The directions are mixed: 8 negative and 10
positive. With 4,000 paired streams per cell, rejection is expected for
any effect of practical size, so the information is in the signs, the
effect sizes and the SESOI classes rather than in the rejections.

\textbf{Invalidation rule.} EXP-001 rejected \(H_0\) for both rules with
positive estimates. At demand times 0.8 and 1.25 every interval lies
above zero (OCC {[}111.9, 153.4{]} and {[}1,084.5, 1,171.2{]}; DRP

\textbf{Beyond the rule.} Against the base-tuned FIX, the advantage
grows when demand exceeds the forecast (up to +18.42\% at x1.6, where
FIX availability falls to 0.807) and reverses when demand falls to x0.6.

x1.25 and x1.6 among the demand-level cells; they lose clearly at x0.6
(-7.47\% and -8.52\%), are within the SESOI at x0.8, and without shocks
OCC loses (-1.19\%) while DRP gains below the SESOI (+0.95\%). With
reversed arrivals DRP is practically equivalent to FIX while OCC gains
+7.30\%.

\section{6. Discussion}\label{discussion}

\textbf{What the evidence supports.} Within this model, the advantage of
simple dynamic rules over a well-tuned fixed price depends on how scarce
the stock is relative to demand. At the base cell the gain is a few
percent, consistent with a small finite-scale gap to the asymptotically
optimal fixed price (Gallego and van Ryzin, 1994); the asymptotic regime
itself is not tested. When expected arrivals equal capacity, both rules
lose at every valuation dispersion, and DRP loses more than OCC in each
of those cells. When arrivals are four times capacity, both rules gain
at every dispersion.

\textbf{Mechanisms.} Two observations explain most of the pattern, and
both are model-dependent inferences.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \emph{Where the gain comes from.} At the base cell the exploratory
  tercile split (B3) shows that most of the average gain arises in
  streams with high realised demand, where the fixed price sells out
  early (85.5\% of the top tercile) and the rules sell the same number
  of units at higher prices. In low-demand streams the rules gain by
  selling stock that would otherwise perish. The M3 report of EXP-001
  named only the second channel; the audit withdrew that reading. The
  no-shocks cell of EXP-003 points the same way: without demand shocks,
  the gain over a correctly tuned fixed price largely disappears (OCC
  -1.19\%, DRP +0.95\%), so much of the base advantage is a response to
  demand uncertainty.
\item
  \emph{Why loose capacity hurts.} In the three \(\kappa = 1.0\) cells
  the tuned fixed price sits where the purchase elasticity is close to
  -1 (-1.253, -1.047, -0.955). When stock does not bind, revenue per
  arriving buyer is \(p \cdot P(v \geq p)\), which is maximised where
  the elasticity equals -1, so the fixed price is already near the
  unconstrained optimum and there is little scarcity to exploit. DRP's
  target asks it to clear the remaining stock by the deadline; with
  loose capacity the target is out of reach, and the multiplicative
  update keeps lowering the price over 60 periods even at
  \(\eta = 0.025\) (mean price paid 81.6 against 100.48 in sv0.5-k1.0).
  The same clearance logic explains the losses at demand x0.6 in
  EXP-003.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Competing explanations.} Table 8 lists, for each confirmatory
conclusion, the competing explanations named in the protocols and how
far the results address them.

\textbf{Second review pass.} A pass that argued against the preferred
reading (\texttt{research/publication/review\_pass\_2.md}) led to four
revisions, all recorded: the EXP-001 mechanism was corrected; the
EXP-002 lower-edge reading was qualified by the realised DRP prices; the
FIX6 check was reclassified as one-sided; and the EXP-003 invalidation
rule is now described as a test against an equally misspecified fixed
price, which is weaker than a test of structural advantage.

\textbf{Practical significance.} The findings bound what a simulation of
this kind can say. A seller who can tune a fixed price on the correct
demand level loses little by not using these simple rules unless stock
is scarce or demand can surprise upward. A seller facing loose capacity
loses revenue with a clearance-seeking rule such as DRP. These
statements hold for the synthetic market only.

\section{7. Limitations and threats to
validity}\label{limitations-and-threats-to-validity}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Simulation only.} All data are synthetic. Nothing here is
  evidence about any real market, airline, hotel or proprietary pricing
  system, and no fare is predicted.
\item
  \textbf{Behavioural assumptions.} Buyers are myopic, have unit demand
  and never return or compare sellers. Strategic waiting (Su, 2007) can
  change price paths and welfare. There is one seller, no competition,
  no costs and zero salvage.
\item
  \textbf{Arbitrary parameters.} Segment shares, medians, shock sizes
  and the horizon are planning choices, not calibrated estimates.
  EXP-002 and EXP-003 probe only a few directions, one factor at a time.
\item
  \textbf{Policy families as gridded.} Each family is measured on its
  frozen 36-configuration grid. 8 of 18 rule optima in EXP-002 lie on an
  edge; at upper edges the rule may be understated, and at the DRP lower
  edge the rule still moves prices substantially. The grids do not
  include the nesting values \(k = 0\) and \(\eta = 0\). No
  dynamic-programming reference was computed (owner decision), so the
  distance to the optimal policy is unknown.
\item
  \textbf{Statistical.} The EXP-002 permutation \(p\)-values sit at
  their floor, so the Holm values are bounds. Interaction contrasts,
  secondary metrics and EXP-003 intervals are unadjusted and
  descriptive. The M4 checks are exploratory and post hoc, and B1 is
  in-sample on tuning streams.
\item
  \textbf{Construct.} Revenue is the tuning objective, so a comparison
  on revenue is fair to each family on its own terms but says nothing
  about other objectives. The consumer surplus proxy rests on synthetic
  valuations. ``Elasticity'' is operationalised by \(\sigma_v\), while
  the realised elasticity also depends on the tuned price.
\item
  \textbf{Execution.} The confirmatory runs shared a loaded machine with
  other sessions; timings are not results. Raw per-run outputs are
  git-ignored and must be regenerated to re-audit them.
\item
  \textbf{Literature.} The search was targeted, not systematic; one of
  the four cited sources (Elmaghraby and Keskinocak, 2003) was read as
  an abstract only.
\end{itemize}

The living list is \texttt{research/limitations.md}.

\section{8. Ethics and responsible
research}\label{ethics-and-responsible-research}

The study uses synthetic data only; no personal data was collected and
no human participant was involved, so no ethics approval was needed or
claimed. No website was scraped and no proprietary system was probed.
The claims boundary excludes airline personalisation claims, live
scraping and actual fare predictions. The consumer surplus proxy is a
property of synthetic agents, not a welfare measurement of people, and
the results should not be read as guidance on charging real customers.
The study evaluates availability and buyer-side outcomes as outcomes,
not as targets for manipulation.

\section{9. Conclusion and future
work}\label{conclusion-and-future-work}

In a transparent, preregistered simulation of a perishable stock, simple
occupancy and demand-responsive pricing rules earn 3.47\% and 3.94\%
more than the best fixed price at the base scenario. That advantage is
conditional. It reverses in every loose-capacity cell, grows with
demand-to-capacity tightness, survives moderate demand misspecification
against an equally misspecified fixed price, and against a correctly
re-tuned fixed price remains practically relevant only when demand
exceeds the forecast or, for OCC, when the arrival order is reversed.
Within this model, and for these two rule families, the value of dynamic
pricing lies in responding to scarcity and to demand above the forecast,
not in changing prices as such. Other dynamic rules, in particular a
known-model optimal policy, were not tested and could behave
differently.

Feasible extensions, each needing a new experiment identifier and the
owner's approval: grids that include the nesting values \(k = 0\) and
\(\eta = 0\); a FIX6 arm in every cell; a known-model
dynamic-programming reference; combined demand shifts or tuning on a
mixture of demand levels; and strategic buyers.

\section{10. Data, code and artifact
availability}\label{data-code-and-artifact-availability}

All code, protocols, configurations, committed summaries and figures are
in the project repository
(https://github.com/mohamedbechirkefi/fare-dynamic-pricing); the
interactive demo is hosted at
https://fare-dynamic-pricing.kefimohamedbechir.workers.dev. Key paths:
\texttt{research/protocol.md}, \texttt{research/freeze.json},
\texttt{research/experiments/EXP-NNN/} (protocol, report, configuration,
run manifest, summary, metrics, figures, reproduction notes),
\texttt{research/publication/artifact\_manifest.json} and
\texttt{research/publication/evidence\_audit.md}. From the repository
root:

\begin{verbatim}
UV=/path/to/uv
$UV sync --frozen
PYTHONPATH=src $UV run python -m pytest -q
PYTHONPATH=src $UV run python -m fare.cli run --config research/experiments/EXP-001/config.json --out results/raw/confirmatory
PYTHONPATH=src $UV run python -m fare.summary --result results/raw/confirmatory/<run_set_id>/result.json --out research/experiments/EXP-001
PYTHONPATH=src $UV run python -m fare.audit research/paper/manuscript.md
\end{verbatim}

Replace EXP-001 by EXP-002 or EXP-003 for the other experiments
(EXP-003's summary also takes
\texttt{-\/-exp001-summary\ research/experiments/EXP-001/summary.json}).
The repository is source-available under a non-commercial research
licence chosen by the owner. A clean-clone reproduction (locked install,
test suite, smoke run and demo build) was performed at the
release-candidate milestone; its commands and actual outputs are in
\texttt{research/publication/reproducibility\_report.md}.

\section{11. Funding, competing interests and AI
assistance}\label{funding-competing-interests-and-ai-assistance}

\textbf{Funding.} No funding was received.

\textbf{Competing interests.} The author declares no competing
interests.

\textbf{AI assistance.} The author used an AI research and development
assistant (Claude Code, Anthropic) under the author's direction. The
assistant proposed the draft protocols, wrote the simulation code and
tests, ran the frozen experiments, composed the experiment reports,
performed the evidence audit and drafted this manuscript. The author set
the research question, approved the protocol amendments, froze the
protocols, approved the authorship metadata and made every recorded
owner decision (\texttt{research/decision\_log.md}). Verification so far
is automated (a test suite, hash checks, a recomputation of every
committed table from the raw outputs and a number trace of this
manuscript) plus the assistant's own second review pass; the author's
review of this draft is pending
(\texttt{research/publication/author\_review.md}). The assistant is not
an author.
